name: Srinagar
tagline: Mughal gardens, houseboats and the still mirror of Dal Lake.
whenBlurb: Come for tulips and gardens in April, gardens and Dal Lake through summer, and chinar colour in autumn; winter is cold, snowbound and hushed.

ourTake.lede: Srinagar is a lake-and-garden city best taken gently, and the classic way in is a night or two on a well-kept houseboat on Dal or, better, the quieter Nigeen Lake. Do the shikara at dawn for the floating vegetable market and the Mughal gardens in the late afternoon light. Check the situation before you commit, and lean on a good local operator; conditions can change, and local knowledge matters here.
ourTake.comeIf: You want a shikara on Dal Lake, a heritage houseboat and Mughal gardens in bloom.
ourTake.skipIf: You want nightlife or guaranteed year-round access.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: The Lalit Grand Palace Srinagar
items.area: Srinagar (Gupkar / palace grounds, above Dal Lake)
credentials: Former palace of Maharaja Pratap Singh (built 1910), recognised heritage-palace hotel, The Lalit Hotels
Historic site of the Gandhi–Maharaja Hari Singh meeting; former host to Lord Mountbatten
items.description: The Maharaja's own palace, set in 101 acres of chinar-shaded gardens above the Dal, the grandest address in the valley.

items.name: Taj Dal View, Srinagar
items.area: Srinagar (Kralsangri, Brein, Zabarwan hillside above Dal Lake)
credentials: Taj Hotels / IHCL flagship luxury hotel in Srinagar (formerly Vivanta Dal View)
items.description: The Taj flagship of the valley, set high on the Zabarwan hills with the Dal, the Mughal gardens and the Pir Panjal laid out below.

items.name: The Khyber Himalayan Resort & Spa, Gulmarg
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller India Readers' Travel Awards, Favourite Boutique Hotel (multiple years, 2014–2023)
Condé Nast Traveller India, among the top hotels in India for Favourite Indian Leisure Hotel & Favourite Spa in a Hotel
items.description: A timber-and-stone lodge at 8,825 ft in the Pir Panjal, facing the snows of Apharwat, the finest mountain address in Kashmir.

items.name: Butt's Clermont Houseboats
items.area: Srinagar (western Dal Lake, by the Mughal 'Garden of the Morning Breeze')
credentials: Iconic heritage houseboats est. 1947, former host to Lord Mountbatten, Nelson Rockefeller, George Harrison and Ravi Shankar
Recognised J&K Tourism (TIH) registered heritage houseboats
items.description: The most storied houseboats on the Dal, moored under century-old chinars, where George Harrison learned sitar with Ravi Shankar.

items.name: Sukoon Houseboat
credentials: Featured by Condé Nast Traveller and Mr & Mrs Smith, leading luxury houseboat on Dal Lake
items.description: The Dal Lake houseboat reimagined, carved walnut and cream linen, a rooftop terrace and a level of service found nowhere else on the water.

items.name: Welcomhotel by ITC Hotels, Pine N Peak, Pahalgam
credentials: ITC Hotels / Welcomhotel, recognised luxury property, the leading luxury retreat in Pahalgam
items.description: A cedar-and-stone retreat on the Rajwas plateau above the Lidder, the one true luxury address in Pahalgam.

items.name: Vivanta Dal View, Boulevard heritage stays
credentials: Taj group (IHCL) standing on the Dal Lake Boulevard
items.description: The dependable, well-run polish of a global group on the Dal's edge, minutes from the gardens and the shikara ghats.

items.name: A Shikara Ride on Dal Lake
items.description: The slow, cushioned glide of a hand-paddled shikara through the still water at golden hour is the image of Kashmir every Indian carries in their head. Have a private boat held for the family at first light or last light, when the lake empties of day-trippers and the Zabarwan hills turn copper on the surface.

items.name: A Heritage Houseboat Stay
items.description: The carved-cedar houseboats moored on the Dal and the quieter Nagin are a living relic of the Raj, all fretwork panelling, Kashmiri carpets and a verandah that opens straight onto the water. Book a full boat for the family for a night or two as a set-piece, then move to a hotel like the Vivanta or Lalit for the comforts a longer stay wants.

items.name: The Floating Vegetable Market at Dawn
items.description: Before sunrise, growers from the lake's floating gardens gather in a knot of shikaras to trade lotus stems, greens and haakh, bargaining boat-to-boat on the black water. It is the one experience here that rewards an unglamorous alarm; a guide who knows the growers gets you into the ring rather than watching from the edge.

items.name: Char Chinar Island
items.description: A tiny island in the Dal marked by four great chinar trees at its corners, laid out by a Mughal prince and unchanged in feel for centuries. Paddle out by shikara for kahwa under the plane trees, with the whole amphitheatre of lake, houseboats and mountains around you.

items.name: Nagin Lake
items.description: The Dal's clearer, quieter sister, ringed by willows and the calmest houseboats in the valley. Families who want the Dal's romance without its bustle base themselves here; the swimming and the stillness make it the connoisseur's address in Srinagar.

items.name: Shalimar Bagh
credentials: On UNESCO's World Heritage Tentative List as part of the serial 'Mughal Gardens in Kashmir' nomination
items.description: Jahangir's garden of love, built in 1619 for the empress Nur Jahan, its central water channel stepping down through terraces of chinar shade to the Dal below. It is the grandest of the Mughal gardens and the one that most fully explains why the emperors called Kashmir paradise.

items.name: Nishat Bagh
credentials: On UNESCO's World Heritage Tentative List as part of the serial 'Mughal Gardens in Kashmir' nomination
items.description: The 'garden of gladness', a twelve-terraced sweep on the eastern shore of the Dal, laid out in 1633 with the Zabarwan range rising directly behind it and the lake spread out in front. The most dramatically sited of all the gardens; go late afternoon when the light rakes across the terraces.

items.name: Chashme Shahi
credentials: On UNESCO's World Heritage Tentative List as part of the serial 'Mughal Gardens in Kashmir' nomination
items.description: The smallest and most intimate of the Mughal gardens, built around a natural spring whose cold, sweet water is still bottled and carried home by Kashmiris for its reputed purity. A short, gentle visit with a fine view down over the Dal, easily paired with the tulip garden and Pari Mahal just above.

items.name: Pari Mahal at Sunset
credentials: On UNESCO's World Heritage Tentative List as part of the serial 'Mughal Gardens in Kashmir' nomination
items.description: The terraced 'palace of the fairies', a former Sufi library and observatory cut into the mountainside above Chashme Shahi, with the finest single view in Srinagar: the whole Dal, the city and the encircling hills laid out below. Come as the light goes and the lamps of the city begin to answer the last of the sun.

items.name: The Naseem Bagh Chinars
items.description: A grove of some 700 towering chinar trees planted by the Mughals on the Dal's shore, now within the university campus and largely free of crowds. Walking its cathedral of plane trees, especially when they burn red in autumn, is the quiet, knowing counterpoint to the famous gardens.

items.name: Hazratbal Shrine
items.description: Kashmir's holiest Muslim shrine, its white marble dome mirrored in the Dal on the lake's western shore, home to the Moi-e-Muqaddas relic revered across the valley. Even for non-Muslim visitors it is a moving, deeply local place; dress modestly and go with a guide who can read its significance.

items.name: Jamia Masjid, Old City
items.description: Srinagar's great congregational mosque, first built in the 14th century, its vast prayer hall carried on more than 370 deodar pillars around a still courtyard. The wooden Indo-Saracenic architecture is unlike any mosque elsewhere in India and the anchor of any walk through the old city.

items.name: Khanqah-e-Moula
items.description: The valley's oldest and most beautiful Sufi shrine, a river-side confection of carved and painted woodwork, papier-mache ceilings and hanging lamps built where Kashmir's Islam first took root. Non-Muslims view from the exterior and threshold; the craftsmanship alone justifies the stop.

items.name: Old City Heritage Walk
items.description: The lanes of Shehr-e-Khaas, Zaina Kadal, the bridges of the Jhelum, the balconied brick-and-timber houses, the copper bazaars and papier-mache workshops, hold the real, unpolished Srinagar. A knowledgeable private guide turns a maze into a legible thousand-year story of trade, craft and faith.

items.name: Shankaracharya Temple
items.description: An ancient Shiva temple crowning a hill above the city, reached by a long stair or a drive, and named for the philosopher Adi Shankara who is said to have meditated here. The 360-degree view over Srinagar and the Dal is the reward; go early before the haze and the crowds.

items.name: Hari Parbat Fort & Makhdoom Sahib
items.description: The Afghan-era fort crowns a hill sacred to all three of Kashmir's faiths, ringed by the Sharika Devi temple, the Makhdoom Sahib Sufi shrine and a gurudwara on its slopes. A short, layered pilgrimage that captures the syncretic soul of old Srinagar in one climb.

items.name: SPS Museum (Sri Pratap Singh Museum)
items.description: The valley's principal museum, founded in 1898, with tens of thousands of objects: Kashmiri shawls and papier-mache, ancient sculpture, coins and Gandhara-era pieces. An hour here gives the crafts you will see in the bazaars their proper historical depth.

items.name: A Wazwan Feast
items.description: The multi-course royal Kashmiri banquet, rista, rogan josh, gushtaba and the rest, traditionally up to thirty-six dishes served on the shared copper trami, is the region's great table ritual, honed over generations of master wazas. Arrange a proper hosted Wazwan (a substantial vegetarian version can be laid on) as the centrepiece meal of the trip.

items.name: Kahwa & the Bakery Culture
items.description: The saffron-and-almond green tea called kahwa, poured from a samovar against the cold, and the morning kandur bakeries with their salt-tea breads, girda, lavasa, sheermal, are the small daily rituals that define Kashmiri hospitality. A guide can walk you into a working bakery at dawn, tea glass in hand.

items.name: Pashmina & Kani Shawl Shopping
credentials: Kashmir Pashmina and Kani Shawl both hold India's Geographical Indication (GI) tag
items.description: The genuine article, hand-spun pashm woven on a Kashmiri loom, or the intricate Kani shawl worked stitch-by-stitch on wooden spokes, is one of the finest textiles on earth and an heirloom purchase. Buy only through a trusted, GI-verified house; a private guide keeps you clear of the machine-made pretenders that flood the market.

items.name: Kashmir Carpets & Crewel
credentials: Kashmir Carpet holds India's Geographical Indication (GI) tag
items.description: Hand-knotted silk and wool carpets in Persian-derived patterns, and the chain-stitched crewel and namda work that dresses Kashmiri homes, are among the valley's signature crafts. The best ateliers will show you the knot count and the design cards; a considered carpet is the trip's grandest souvenir.

items.name: Walnut Wood & Papier-Mache
credentials: Kashmir Walnut Wood Carving and Kashmir Papier Mache both hold India's Geographical Indication (GI) tag
items.description: Kashmir's dark, close-grained walnut is carved into furniture and screens by families who have done it for generations, while papier-mache is painted in fine gold-flecked florals on boxes and panels. Both are GI-protected crafts best bought at the workshop, where you can watch the making.

items.name: Indira Gandhi Memorial Tulip Garden (Seasonal)
credentials: The largest tulip garden in Asia
items.description: For a few weeks from mid-March to April, seven terraces below the Zabarwan range blaze with well over a million tulips in scores of colours, framed by the Dal below. It opens for the annual Tulip Festival; time a spring trip to it and little else in the valley compares.

items.name: Badamwari Almond Blossom (Seasonal)
items.description: In February and early March, before anything else in the valley stirs, this historic almond garden at the foot of Hari Parbat breaks into pink-and-white blossom, Kashmir's first sign of spring. A quiet, uncrowded pleasure that most itineraries miss entirely.

items.name: Royal Springs Golf Course
credentials: Rated the No.1 golf course in India by Golf Digest
items.description: A Robert Trent Jones Jr. course laid along the slopes above the Dal, consistently rated among India's very best and one of the most scenic in Asia. A round here, chinars and lake below and snow peaks beyond, is a rare thing to do on a Kashmir morning.

items.name: Gulmarg: The Gondola to Apharwat
credentials: Among the highest cable cars in the world (world's second-highest / Asia's highest passenger ropeway)
items.description: The two-stage cable car climbs from the Gulmarg meadow to nearly 4,000 metres on the shoulder of Apharwat Peak, one of the highest passenger ropeways in the world with a Himalayan panorama at the top. Do both phases on a clear morning; carry warm layers even in summer, as it is another world up there.

items.name: Gulmarg: The Meadow & Golf Course
credentials: Gulmarg Golf Course is the world's highest green golf course
items.description: The 'meadow of flowers' is a vast bowl of alpine grass ringed by the Pir Panjal, and in summer its greens make up the highest golf course in the world. An easy, glorious day-trip base from Srinagar for families, with pony rides, walks and views in every direction.

items.name: Gulmarg: Skiing & Snow (Winter)
items.description: In winter Gulmarg becomes one of Asia's serious ski destinations, with genuine high-altitude powder off Apharwat reached by the gondola, plus gentle nursery slopes for first-timers and children. Arrange instructors and gear in advance; the off-piste here draws skiers from around the world.

items.name: Pahalgam: The Lidder Valley
items.description: The 'valley of shepherds' sits where the glacier-fed Lidder river runs cold and clear through pine and meadow, the classic Kashmiri summer retreat two-and-a-half hours from Srinagar. It makes a superb overnight base, riverside luxury stays, gentle walks and cool air, for families escaping the plains' heat.

items.name: Pahalgam: Betaab Valley
items.description: A wide green bowl where pine forests meet the Lidder, named for the Bollywood film shot here and postcard-perfect in every direction. An easy, level, kid-friendly stop that delivers the archetypal Kashmir meadow with almost no walking.

items.name: Pahalgam: Aru Valley
items.description: A hushed hamlet and meadow upriver from Pahalgam, the trailhead for the Kolahoi glacier and the Tarsar–Marsar lakes and far quieter than the main town. The place to base for a day of gentle riverside walks or a serious trek with a private outfitter.

items.name: Pahalgam: Chandanwari
items.description: The end of the motorable road up the Lidder, where snow lingers into summer and the annual Amarnath pilgrimage traditionally sets off on foot. A scenic drive to a high, cold, dramatic spot with a taste of the sacred geography beyond.

items.name: Sonamarg: The Meadow of Gold
items.description: 'Meadow of gold', a high alpine bowl at around 2,700 metres on the road to Ladakh, where the Sindh river braids through grass under snow-streaked peaks. The most alpine-feeling of the valley's day-trips and the classic launch point for river rafting and pony rides.

items.name: Sonamarg: Thajiwas Glacier
items.description: A short pony ride or walk from Sonamarg brings you to the snout of the Thajiwas glacier, ringed by conifers and meadows and holding snow through much of the year. A rare chance to stand at a glacier with children in tow, no serious trekking required.

items.name: Yusmarg
items.description: A quiet, rolling meadow of pines and open grass south-west of Srinagar that the crowds still largely skip, its name meaning 'meadow of Jesus'. The hidden-gem alternative to Gulmarg for a family picnic day, all space and silence and horse rides.

items.name: Doodhpathri
items.description: The 'valley of milk', an emerald meadow laced by a shallow, milk-white stream about an hour and a half from Srinagar, still one of Kashmir's least-spoilt escapes. Come for a slow, uncrowded day on the grass, the antidote to the well-trodden circuit.

items.name: The Jhelum Riverfront & Seven Bridges
items.description: The Jhelum threads the heart of the old city under a chain of historic bridges, the kadals, with tall timber-and-brick houses leaning over the water. A walk or a boat along it reads the older, workaday Srinagar that the lakes politely hide.

items.name: Manasbal Lake
items.description: The deepest lake in Kashmir, an hour north of the city, quiet and mirror-still with lotus blooming across it in summer and a small Mughal garden on its shore. A serene, birdwatcher's day-trip almost no tourist itinerary bothers with.

items.name: Wular Lake & the Kashmir Backwaters
items.description: One of the largest freshwater lakes in Asia, fed by the Jhelum and fringed by the villages of north Kashmir, vast and thinly visited. A guided trip out here, birdlife, fishing hamlets, open water under the mountains, is for travellers who have already done the classics.

items.name: Verinag Spring
credentials: On UNESCO's World Heritage Tentative List as part of the serial 'Mughal Gardens in Kashmir' nomination
items.description: The deep, octagonal Mughal-walled spring that is the chief source of the Jhelum, ringed by chinars and remarkably peaceful, south of Srinagar on the Pahalgam road. A worthwhile detour that completes the story of the Mughals' love affair with Kashmir's water.

items.name: Achabal Bagh
credentials: On UNESCO's World Heritage Tentative List as part of the serial 'Mughal Gardens in Kashmir' nomination
items.description: A serene Mughal spring-garden laid out for Nur Jahan around a powerful natural spring, with cascades, chinar avenues and far fewer visitors than the Srinagar gardens. A graceful, unhurried stop that pairs naturally with a run down towards Pahalgam.

items.name: The Amarnath Pilgrim Context
items.description: Each summer hundreds of thousands make the high-altitude yatra to the Amarnath ice-lingam cave, staging from Pahalgam's Chandanwari or Sonamarg's Baltal, a sacred rhythm that shapes the valley's whole season. Even without doing the trek, understanding it, and perhaps a helicopter darshan for the devout, is part of reading Kashmir honestly.

items.name: Saffron Fields of Pampore (Seasonal)
credentials: Kashmir Saffron holds India's Geographical Indication (GI) tag
items.description: The plateau around Pampore, minutes outside Srinagar, grows the world-renowned Kashmiri saffron, and for a fortnight each late autumn the fields turn purple with crocus at harvest. A short, vivid seasonal detour, and the place to buy the real, GI-tagged spice at source.

items.name: Dachigam National Park
items.description: A protected valley half an hour from the city and the last refuge of the endangered hangul, the Kashmir stag, alongside black bears and leopards in wooded slopes above the Dal. A permitted, guided visit is a rare wildlife dimension to a trip most people spend entirely on lakes and gardens.

items.name: Kashmiri Cuisine Beyond Wazwan
items.description: Past the grand banquet lies an everyday table worth exploring, haakh greens, nadru (lotus stem), morel mushrooms, the sour-red mujj chetin, and the lake's own fish, much of it deeply vegetarian-friendly. A guided food morning, from bakery to tea-house to home kitchen, is its own small journey.

items.name: Autumn Chinar Season (Seasonal)
items.description: For a few weeks in late October and November the valley's chinars turn crimson and gold, Naseem Bagh, the Mughal gardens, the university, whole avenues ablaze, in what Kashmiris call the harud. The quietest, most photogenic and most underrated time to come.

items.name: The Chinar at The Lalit Grand Palace
credentials: Inside The Lalit Grand Palace, recognised heritage-palace hotel, former Maharaja's residence
Noted for introducing a full and a vegetarian Wazwan (Rista, Modur Pulav, Gushtaba)
items.description: The grand Wazwan, served in the Maharaja's palace with the gardens and Dal beyond, the most refined Kashmiri feast in the city.

items.name: Ahdoos
credentials: Legendary institution est. 1918, widely regarded as the benchmark for authentic Kashmiri Wazwan
items.description: The century-old benchmark of Kashmiri cooking, Persian carpets, old Srinagar photographs, and Wazwan as it should be.

items.name: Mughal Darbar
credentials: Long-running recognised Srinagar institution, among the most-cited Wazwan houses in the city
items.description: A city institution for the full spread, Wazwan-e-Khas and the finest cuts, done with real skill and no fuss.

items.name: Shamyana
credentials: Recognised Boulevard-Road Wazwan restaurant, consistently cited among Srinagar's best for Kashmiri cuisine
items.description: Authentic Kashmiri cooking a step from the Dal, Tabak Maaz, seekh kebabs and Rogan Josh with the lake at the door.

items.name: Krishna Dhaba
credentials: Legendary institution est. 1937, Srinagar's best-known pure-vegetarian address (Krishna Vaishno Dhaba)
items.description: The valley's beloved pure-vegetarian institution, jam-packed, unpretentious, and famous for its dal makhani.

items.name: Houseboat evening on the Dal
credentials: Signature Srinagar evening, heritage Dal Lake houseboats (Butt's Clermont est. 1947; Sukoon, Condé Nast Traveller / Mr & Mrs Smith)
items.description: The valley's true night out, kahwa and dinner on your own carved-walnut deck as the lake goes silent and the hills fade to dark.

items.name: Hotel lounge nightcap
items.area: Srinagar (The Lalit Grand Palace / Taj Dal View)
credentials: Inside recognised luxury hotels, The Lalit Grand Palace (former Maharaja's palace) and Taj Dal View (IHCL)
items.description: A quiet drink in a heritage-palace or hilltop-hotel lounge, the calmest, most civilised late hour in the city.

plan.heading: 4 days in Srinagar, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Arrive and board a heritage houseboat on Nigeen lake, the quieter of the two waters.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A shikara at dusk across Dal, past the floating gardens and kingfishers.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Wazwan dinner aboard, or at Ahdoos in town for the classic Kashmiri table.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Nishat and Shalimar Bagh in the morning cool, the chinars and terraced water channels.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Pari Mahal above the lake and the Hazratbal shrine along the shore.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Return to the houseboat; a quiet supper with the lake still.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Jamia Masjid with its deodar pillars and the Shah-e-Hamdan shrine in the old quarter.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Visit a trusted pashmina and carpet atelier to see the weaving and kani work first-hand.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Mughal Darbar or a private wazwan arranged through your host.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Drive out to Pahalgam and the Lidder valley, or Gulmarg for the gondola and the meadows.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A walk among the pines and a picnic lunch in the open.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Return to Srinagar for a last night on the water, or fly out.

items.name: Nigeen Lake
items.description: The calmer, cleaner lake with the best houseboats; best for a serene base.

items.name: Dal Lake (Boulevard side)
items.description: The famous, busier lake with shikaras and gardens close by; suits first-timers wanting the classic view.

items.name: Old City / Downtown
items.description: The historic heart of shrines, mosques and craft workshops; for those wanting heritage and texture.

events.name: Tulip Festival
events.note: Asia's largest tulip garden below the Zabarwan hills blooms for a few weeks; the signature spring event.

events.name: Almond blossom season
events.note: The Badamwari garden's almond trees flower, marking the first sign of the Kashmiri spring.

events.name: Saffron harvest (Pampore, nearby)
events.note: The purple crocus fields around Pampore bloom for the world's most prized saffron; a rare sight.

events.name: Shikara Festival
events.note: A summer lake festival with decorated-boat races and cultural events on Dal Lake.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: Stay on the quieter Nigeen Lake rather than the busier Dal for privacy; dress is conservative given local custom; the finest pashmina and saffron are bought through your host to avoid the tourist markets, and the Chinar valley is loveliest in autumn.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Srinagar international airport and be met by a private car for the short transfer to the Dal Lake; the elegant arrival is by shikara across the water to a heritage houseboat or lakeside property.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private driver covers the city and day trips to Gulmarg, Pahalgam and Sonamarg, while a shikara is the graceful way to move on Dal and Nigeen lakes.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Only postpaid Indian SIMs are permitted to work in Kashmir; prepaid and many eSIMs will not connect, so arrange a postpaid line or rely on hotel wifi.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Indian rupee; carry cash for shikaras, markets and craft purchases, though hotels and better shops take cards; modest tipping is appreciated.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: April–October is lovely: tulips and almond blossom in spring, gardens and Dal Lake in summer, chinar-gold in October. Avoid December–February unless you want deep cold and snow (beautiful, but flights and roads get unreliable).

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Direct from Delhi to Srinagar (SXR) in about 90 minutes, and from Mumbai in ~2.5hrs; Air India and IndiGo fly it well, Air India offering a business cabin on some Delhi frequencies. Take a morning slot, afternoon weather closes the valley, and use the Delhi lounge, as SXR itself is functional, not plush.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations beyond routine. Honestly: the valley is open and safe for tourism in 2026, with record arrivals and a strong tourist-police presence on the Srinagar–Gulmarg–Pahalgam circuit, stay to established routes and a vetted local operator. Srinagar is low-altitude and gentle; water sealed/bottled only.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Easy for vegetarian, and Jain is manageable with notice. Kashmiri cuisine is meat-heavy (the Wazwan), but haak, nadru (lotus stem) and rich vegetarian dishes are excellent; pure-veg and Jain kitchens exist in the city and every good hotel/houseboat will cook to order. Ask your houseboat or property to prep Jain in advance rather than improvising out.
